articles.title: How to Check Locked Tokens in a Wallet Address (Any Chain)
articles.excerpt: To check locked tokens in a wallet address, open the chain's block explorer, look up the address, and read the balance breakdown: most explorers show "available" separately from "locked", "reserved",…
articles.body: To check locked tokens in a wallet address, open the chain's block explorer, look up the address, and read the balance breakdown: most explorers show "available" separately from "locked", "reserved", "frozen", "staked" or "in escrow". If the explorer only shows a total, you then check the contracts the wallet has interacted with (staking, vesting, escrow) to see what holds the rest and when it unlocks. This guide walks through that process chain by chain, explains the common lock types, and shows how to tell a normal lock from a genuinely stuck balance. You need nothing but the public address. You never need a seed phrase, a private key or a wallet connection to read a balance. What "locked tokens" actually means "Locked" is an umbrella word.

articles.title: How to check for Go MPTCP listeners and turn them off
articles.excerpt: Originally published on ImportStatic. Turning off Multipath TCP in a Go server removes the condition the published exploit for CVE-2026-98432 needs, but it leaves the kernel bug in place. Anthropic de…
articles.body: Originally published on ImportStatic . Turning off Multipath TCP in a Go server removes the condition the published exploit for CVE-2026-98432 needs, but it leaves the kernel bug in place. Anthropic described that exploit on October 27 as zero-click remote code execution against Linux servers with an MPTCP listener, and since Go 1.24 a Go server on Linux has opened its listening sockets with MPTCP unless you told it otherwise. The Go Security Team's notice followed on October 30, and a Hacker News thread took up whether turning MPTCP off in Go protects you. The bug is in the kernel's IPv4 TCP code, and the Go team's post warns that systems without MPTCP listeners may be open to similar attacks.

articles.title: Who wrote this code? AI provenance starts with the wrong question
articles.excerpt: Originally published at getlockstep.dev. A customer loses access to a feature after a pricing change. The code path is easy to find. git blame points to a commit from three weeks ago. The commit is cl…
articles.body: Originally published at getlockstep.dev . A customer loses access to a feature after a pricing change. The code path is easy to find. git blame points to a commit from three weeks ago. The commit is clean: one eligibility condition changed, tests updated, pull request approved. The diff was written by an AI coding agent, but the commit sits under an engineer's name because that is how the work entered the repository. Now answer the question the customer actually forced onto the table: why did eligibility change? The commit message says "update plan checks." The issue says "align with new pricing." The agent transcript is gone. The Slack thread contains four proposals and no obvious verdict. Product remembers agreeing to one exception. Engineering remembers a different one.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

articles.excerpt: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?
articles.body: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
